newsitem.title: MEXICO: Firefighters battle Mexico City fuel blast.
newsitem.headline: Firefighters battle Mexico City fuel blast.

text.p: Hundreds of firefighters battled to contain a dangerous blaze early on Tuesday at a fuel storage facility owned by state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) just outside Mexico City.
Towering columns of flame lit up the capital's night sky more than 12 hours after a giant fuel storage tank exploded in this city suburb, injuring at least 11 and forcing thousands from their homes.

Flames rose hundreds of yards (metres) into the air after the initial blast on Monday afternoon quickly spread to a second storage tank, adding to the immense inferno. Heavy smoke from the blaze blanketed much of the city.

Throughout the night, firefighters sprayed cold water and fire-retardant chemicals on other tanks nearby in an effort to prevent them from igniting as well. Television images showed dozens of dazed firefighters, some struggling to stay on their feet, being treated for smoke inhalation by Red Cross workers.

Pemex officials said the blaze, although still huge, was under control by late on Monday and would die out sometime on Tuesday after some 105,000 barrels of gasoline stored in the two tanks burned out. They said firefighters were using 8,000 gallons (30,000 liters) of water per second to control the fire.
But a Reuter photographer and other eyewitnesses on Tuesday said the blaze suddenly flared during the night as heavy wind gusts fanned the fire.
"The winds are against us. The fire is mostly under control, but this is a tough battle," an unidentified fireman told Mexico City's Radio Red.

Other tanks in the facility contained as much as 1.25 million gallons (4.7 million liters) of gasoline each, but were being slowly drained during the night to prevent new explosions, officials at the oil giant said.
Pemex director Adrian Lajous arrived to tour the site on Tuesday and said special fire-fighting equipment was being sent in from Pemex's facilities in other parts of Mexico.

Army troops and state police evacuated up to 1,000 people from the area earlier on Monday and sympathetic Mexico City residents called local radio stations to offer shelter to those forced from their homes. Schools within 1.4 miles (two km) of the storage facility were cancelled for Tuesday.
An unknown number of residents were treated for smoke inhalation and many complained of a burning sensation in their eyes, witnesses said.
"We heard a loud noise, we didn't know what it was. Then we saw the fire," said a shaken Lourdes Rivas Mendoza, a 30-year-old housewife who lives near the site of the blast.
As the smoke poured into the air late on Monday, Mexico City health officials urged residents of this already polluted city to avoid outdoor exercise and stay indoors on Tuesday.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, during a visit to Chile on Monday for a summit of regional leaders, ordered federal emergency aid to the area.

For San Juan residents like Rivas, the blast recalled another nearly 12 years ago, when natural gas tanks in the area exploded, killing at least 511 people and injuring thousands. The anniversary of that tragedy is a week away.
TV Azteca television network said local residents had been pressing for some time for the depot to be relocated because of safety concerns.
Monday's explosion occurred at 3:05 p.m. (2105 GMT) at Pemex's storage and distribution center in this industrial suburb, some 11 miles (16 km) from downtown.

Doctors in area hospitals said most victims suffered second- and third-degree burns. Bloodied firemen were seen being taken on stretchers to hospitals, their faces raw with burns and swathed in bandages.

The explosion was the second in recent months at a Pemex installation. On July 26 a blast caused by human error at the firm's Cactus gas processing center in the southern state of Chiapas killed six workers.
